summary: Give the Feed conversion ratio calculator the final animal(s) weight, the weight of milk produced, number of eggs produced and the FCR and it returns initial animal(s) weight. That makes it useful for an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Feed conversion ratio calculator work?
sections.html:
The Feed conversion ratio calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports initial animal(s) weight in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the product type); then you type in the final animal(s) weight, the weight of milk produced, number of eggs produced and the FCR (meat).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Feed conversion ratio calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Initial animal(s) weight=final animal(s) weight − total weight gain by the animal(s)
Total weight of the live animals=total weight of slaughtered animals + total weight of animal by-products
Total feed consumed=economic FCR × total weight of slaughtered animals
Technical FCR=total feed consumed ÷ number of animals that left the farmhouse
Total weight gain by the animal(s)=total feed consumed ÷ FCR (meat)
Total feed consumed=FCR (milk) × weight of milk produced

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Feed conversion ratio calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the final animal(s) weight, the weight of milk produced and number of eggs produced — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Feed conversion ratio calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns initial animal(s) weight, derived from the final animal(s) weight, the weight of milk produced and number of eggs produced. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Feed conversion ratio calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the final animal(s) weight, the weight of milk produced, number of eggs produced and the FCR, which is 14 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total feed consumed (Feed conversion ratio (FCR)) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total feed consumed (Feed conversion ratio (FCR)) opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Feed conversion ratio calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
